title: Minute Clock
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the time chapter. An adult sees a clock being read, which a paper plate clock does well. What is actually being settled is where the minutes are counted from and which hour is read. The chapter's own clocks are drawn up to a mark away from the times the text gives them, and the book's key reads one exercise face a minute off. So this tool draws every hand exactly, and the plan accepts a reading of the printed faces within one minute. The hour hand is the other trap: late in an hour it is almost on the next number, and the hour is still the one it has passed.

writeup.why: Read an analog clock to the exact minute, and set its two hands for any time, knowing where each hand has to point.
writeup.look: A large clock face with sixty marks and two hands, a digital readout beside it, and a ring of fives round the face that can be shown or hidden.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Minute Clock' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the clocks read or set against the clocks this phase holds, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each time is written or each pair of hands settles, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The clock face fills the left of the working area, a disc 480 across centred at 330,466, on the panel colour with a near-black rim: the twelve numbers upright in their usual places, sixty minute marks round the rim and a longer mark at every number. The minute hand is long and deep blue and reaches the marks; the hour hand is short, thicker and vermilion; both turn from one near-black hub. The fives ring sits just outside the rim, 512 across, writing five, ten, fifteen and on to sixty beside the long marks in deep blue, and it can be shown or hidden. The counting arc runs round inside the rim from the twelve and follows the minute hand, lighting in deep blue a block of five marks at a time up to the last number the hand has passed, then the marks after it one at a time. The digital readout stands at the top of the right half, 300 by 110 at 640,226, with a sliding cover. The words card lies under it, 480 by 80 at 640,356, reading the time as minutes past the hour or minutes to the next hour. The magnifier stands under that, 480 by 200 at 640,456: the space between two numbers spread wide, its four small lines drawn tall and its five spaces numbered one to five as they are counted. The hour finder is drawn on the face: it rings the number the hour hand has passed in filled vermilion and outlines the number it is moving towards in near-black. To draw a time, the minute hand is dragged and snaps to the nearest mark, and the hour hand is dragged freely while a pale ghost shows where it belongs for the minutes set, thirty degrees for each hour and half a degree for each minute past it. Where a child has set the minute hand, a pale ghost of it can show where that hand belongs. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve keys three across, the ten digits, a colon and a clear key, and the answer slot holds a time as the hour, a colon and two places for the minutes, both places drawn on every time so that a minute below ten is written with a nought in front. On the second and third phases the slot takes a number of minutes alone, with the word minutes under it. Where a phase asks for a clock to be drawn, the slot shows the written time and the hands on the face are the answer. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The hour hand, every hour tile and hour cell, the hours column, and the hours of a time the stage splits into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand, every minute tile and minute cell, the minutes column and the minutes of a split time are deep blue. The second hand, every second cell and the seconds column are reddish purple. The a.m. half of the day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on a track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every clock rim, minute mark, clock number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket, guide line and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined, before any of them is told by a colour. A figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. Every hand on this stage is drawn exactly for its time, so the hour hand stands on a number only when the minutes are nought, and the minute hand points exactly at a mark. A reading of the book's printed faces within one minute is accepted, because those faces are drawn up to a mark away from the times their text gives them.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last clock the child set, both hands drawn exactly, with the time in figures and in words underneath.

phases.win: the two clocks agree, and the time is written under both in figures and in words
phases.does: reads the figures, drags the hands until the clock with hands shows the same time, then uncovers the words card
phases.goal: a digital clock shows the time in figures and an analog clock shows it with hands, and both can show the same time to the exact minute
phases.says: This clock shows the time in figures. Can you make the clock with hands show it too?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a digital clock shows 4:10. Where do the two hands of a clock with hands point?
phases.feels: two clocks tell the same moment, one in figures and one by where its hands point
phases.hands: Stand a digital clock or a phone showing the time beside the wall clock, and ask the class to read both and say whether they agree. Then write 4:10 on the board and have each child set it on a paper plate clock. Compare where the hour hands went: on the four, just before it, or just past it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which figures are the hour, and which are the minutes? Second rung, the phase's: which number does the minute hand point at for these minutes? Third rung: the time is cut to an o'clock, the minute hand on the twelve and the hour hand on a number, before the full time comes back. The pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the figures show a five, and the numbers on the face look as if they mean what they say.
wrong.move: points the minute hand at the five for 9:05, taking the five in the figures as the number the hand should point at.
wrong.screen: the words card reads the child's hands back, twenty-five past nine, under the readout's five past nine. The fives ring shows its numbers, five beside the one and twenty-five beside the five, and a pale ghost of the minute hand settles on the one. The child's hand stays on the five beside it, nothing marked.

wrong.why: at nine o'clock the hour hand sits on the nine, and five minutes seems too little to move it.
wrong.move: draws the hour hand for 9:05 exactly on the nine, or just short of it, as if nine o'clock had not quite come.
wrong.screen: the pale ghost of the hour hand settles two and a half degrees past the nine, and the hour finder rings the nine as passed and outlines the ten. The minute hand is swept back to the twelve and on again to the one, and the ghost is seen to leave the nine as it goes. The child's hour hand stays where it was set, beside the ghost.

phases.screen: the analog clock and the digital readout side by side, the readout showing a time and the clock's hands waiting at twelve
phases.soWhat: A digital clock shows the time in figures and an analog clock shows it with hands, and both can show the same time to the exact minute.

phases.win: five spaces light between each pair of numbers, and sixty light round the whole face as one hour
phases.does: counts the spaces between the two numbers, then steps the minute hand on one mark at a time while a count of minutes rises
phases.goal: the space between two numbers has five equal parts, and the minute hand takes one minute to move from one mark to the next
phases.says: Count the spaces from one number to the next. How long does the hand take to cross one space?
phases.check: How many minutes does the minute hand take to go from the eight to the twelve?
phases.feels: the space between two numbers is five small steps, and every step takes one minute
phases.hands: Hold up a paper plate clock and point to the space between the one and the two. Ask how many small spaces there are, then count them together while a child moves the minute hand one mark at a time, and ask how long the hand took. Then count round the whole plate in fives, pointing at each number, up to sixty.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many spaces are there between two numbers? Second rung, the phase's: how long does the hand take to cross one space? Third rung: the magnifier is cut to one stretch, from one number to the next, and the child counts its spaces before the longer stretch comes back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the lines are what is drawn between the numbers, and counting what is drawn feels like counting minutes.
wrong.move: counts the four small lines between two numbers as four minutes, and says the hand takes twelve minutes from the four to the seven.
wrong.screen: the magnifier spreads the space between the four and the five, and its five spaces light and are numbered one to five, the last ending on the long mark at the five. The minute hand then steps from the four to the seven one mark at a time while the count of minutes climbs by one at each mark, to fifteen, and the child's twelve stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the numbers are the large marks on the face, and passing one feels like one step.
wrong.move: says three minutes from the four to the seven, because the hand passed three numbers.
wrong.screen: the magnifier opens on each stretch in turn, four to five, five to six and six to seven, and each lights five spaces. The three stretches stand side by side as three blocks of five, fifteen spaces in all, and the child's three stays in the slot beside the count.

phases.screen: the magnifier over the space between the one and the two, with the minute hand resting on the one
phases.soWhat: Each small mark is one minute, and there are five of them from one number to the next.
phases.concept: Each small mark is a minute

phases.win: the fives light up to that number, the marks after it light one by one, and the minutes are written
phases.does: counts in fives round to the last number the hand has passed, counts the marks after it, then sets the minute hand for a written time
phases.goal: the minutes are counted in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, and then mark by mark
phases.says: Count in fives to the last number the hand has passed. Now count the marks after it.
phases.check: The minute hand is three marks past the eight. How many minutes past the hour is that?
phases.feels: the numbers on the face stand for fives, and only the marks after the last one count in ones
phases.hands: Set a paper plate clock with its minute hand three marks past the seven. Have the class count in fives round to the seven aloud, five, ten, up to thirty-five, then in ones for the marks after it, and write the minutes on the board. Then set the hand exactly on the nine and ask how many minutes that is, and why it is not nine.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number has the minute hand just passed? Second rung, the phase's: how many minutes does that number stand for? Third rung: the hand is set exactly on a number, and the child counts the fives to it before the marks after it come back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the number beside the hand is the one the eye meets, and it is a small number that looks like minutes.
wrong.move: reads the six as six minutes, adds the four marks after it, and answers ten minutes past the hour.
wrong.screen: the fives ring shows its numbers, and thirty stands beside the six. The counting arc runs from the twelve in blocks of five, five, ten and on to thirty at the six, then lights the four marks after it one at a time to thirty-four. The child's ten stays in the slot beside the arc's count.

wrong.why: the hand stands nearer the seven than the six, so the seven looks like the number it belongs to.
wrong.move: counts in fives up to the seven, which the hand is heading for, adds the four marks, and answers thirty-nine.
wrong.screen: the counting arc stops its fives at the six, the last number the hand has passed, and the fives ring lights thirty there. The stretch from the six to the seven is lit mark by mark, and it stops at the fourth mark, one short of the seven. The child's thirty-nine stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the hand points straight at a number, and a hand on a number looks as if it is showing that number.
wrong.move: writes 3:09 for a clock whose minute hand is on the nine and whose hour hand is three quarters of the way from the three to the four.
wrong.screen: the fives ring lights forty-five beside the nine, and the counting arc runs round in nine blocks of five to meet the hand. The words card reads a quarter to four, the readout's cover slides back on 3:45, and the child's 3:09 stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the minute hand set a few marks past a number, with the fives ring hidden
phases.soWhat: Count in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, then count the marks after it.
phases.concept: Counting on from the last number

phases.win: the number behind the hour hand lights, the time is written with that hour, and the words card reads minutes to the next hour
phases.does: reads the minutes, taps the number the hour hand has passed, then drags both hands to draw a written time
phases.goal: the hour is the number the hour hand has passed, not the number it is moving towards
phases.says: The hour hand is nearly at the next number. Which number has it passed?
phases.check: The hour hand is just short of the eleven, and the minute hand is two marks past the eleven. What time is it?
phases.feels: late in an hour the hour hand is nearly at the next number, and it still has not arrived
phases.hands: Draw a clock at twenty to six on the board, its hour hand two thirds of the way from the five to the six, and ask which hour it shows. Let the class argue, then draw six o'clock beside it and ask what the hour hand had to do to get there. Write both times, 5:40 and 6:00.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number has the hour hand passed? Second rung, the phase's: has the minute hand reached the twelve yet? Third rung: the clock is cut to a time early in the hour, with the hour hand just past a number, before the late time comes back. The pad and the hands stay open.

wrong.why: the hour hand is nearer the four than the three, and the nearer number looks like the hour.
wrong.move: reads the hour as four because the hour hand is almost on the four, and writes 4:58.
wrong.screen: the hour finder rings the three as the number passed and outlines the four, and the magnifier spreads the space between the three and the four, where the hour hand's tip is seen one degree short of the four. The minute hand is run on two marks to the twelve, and only then does the hour hand touch the four. The child's 4:58 stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: six is the only hour in a quarter to six, so it goes in front of the colon.
wrong.move: writes 6:45 for a quarter to six, taking the hour named in the words as the hour the hand has passed.
wrong.screen: the clock is set to a quarter to six, the minute hand on the nine and the hour hand three quarters of the way from the five to the six. The hour finder rings the five and outlines the six, and the words card reads fifteen minutes to six. The child's 6:45 is set as a pale second pair of hands, whose hour hand sits three quarters of the way past the six, and both stay side by side.

wrong.why: the time begins with eight, and the eight is where an eight o'clock hand goes.
wrong.move: draws the hour hand for 8:50 right on the eight, where it stands at eight o'clock.
wrong.screen: the pale ghost of the hour hand settles five degrees short of the nine, five sixths of the way from the eight. The minute hand is swept back from the ten to the twelve and the ghost slides back to the eight with it, so the fifty minutes are seen to have carried the hour hand along. The child's hand stays on the eight beside the ghost.

phases.screen: a clock late in an hour, with the hour hand almost on the next number
phases.soWhat: The hour is the number the hour hand has passed, not the one it is nearly at.
phases.concept: The hour the hand has passed

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the minute hand is dragged once all the way round. The hour hand creeps after it the whole time, so slowly that it seems to stand still, and the hour finder's filled ring stays on the number behind it through fifty-nine minutes. The moment the minute hand reaches the twelve, the hour hand touches the next number and the filled ring hops onto it, not a moment before. Dragging back sends both hands back together. It can be tried as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the digital readout shows a time in figures beside the clock, whose two hands wait together at the twelve, and the words card lies face down. On the second the magnifier stands over the space between the one and the two, with the minute hand resting on the one and the count of minutes at nought. On the third the minute hand stands a few marks past a number, with the fives ring hidden and the counting arc unlit. On the fourth the clock shows a time late in an hour, its hour hand almost on the next number, with the hour finder dark and the readout covered. The running count at the top left holds the clocks read or set against the clocks this phase holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the minute hand, or the magnifier, or the tip of the minute hand, or the hour hand, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where each hand is pointing. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any time on the clock, with the readout, the fives ring, the counting arc, the magnifier, the hour finder and the words card all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on digital and analog clocks, counting the marks, counting on from the last number passed, and reading and drawing the hour hand.
voiceLines: A clock with two hands, and a clock with figures. Where is each hand pointing?
This clock shows the time in figures. Can you make the clock with hands show it too?
Count the spaces from one number to the next. How long does the hand take to cross one space?
Count in fives to the last number the hand has passed. Now count the marks after it.
The hour hand is nearly at the next number. Which number has it passed?
A new clock. Find the minute hand before you read anything.
Free play. Any time on the clock, with the ring, the arc, the magnifier and the hour finder open.
Count the fives again, up to the last number the minute hand has passed.
Minutes counted in fives and then marks, and the hour read from the number the hand has passed.

observations.why: Both clocks tell one time; one writes the hours and minutes as figures and the other shows them with two hands.
observations.soWhat: A digital clock shows the time in figures and an analog clock shows it with hands, and both can show the same time to the exact minute.
observations.observe: The clock with hands settled on the same time as the figures, and the words card read it aloud.

observations.why: Four small lines split the space between two numbers into five equal parts, and the hand takes one minute to cross each.
observations.soWhat: Each small mark is one minute, and there are five of them from one number to the next.
observations.observe: Five spaces lit between the one and the two, and sixty lit round the whole face as the minute hand went once round.

observations.why: Each number stands for five minutes more than the one before it, so the last number passed gives the fives and the marks after it give the ones.
observations.soWhat: Count in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, then count the marks after it.
observations.observe: The arc lit in fives up to the six, thirty, and then one mark at a time to thirty-four.

observations.why: The hour hand moves half a degree a minute, and it reaches the four only as the minute hand reaches the twelve.
observations.soWhat: The hour is the number the hour hand has passed, not the one it is nearly at.
observations.observe: At fifty-eight minutes past three the hour hand stood one degree short of the four, and the hour finder rang the three.

source_tool.description: A large analog clock fills the left of the working area, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and a longer mark at every number. Its minute hand is long and its hour hand short, and both are drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees a minute and points exactly at a mark. The hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree a minute, so it moves between two numbers in step with the minutes. A digital readout beside the clock shows the same time in figures and can be covered. A fives ring round the outside of the face numbers the long marks five, ten, fifteen and on to sixty, and can be shown or hidden. A counting arc follows the minute hand. It lights the fives from the twelve up to the last number the hand has passed, then the marks after that number one at a time. A magnifier spreads the space between two numbers apart so its four small lines and five spaces can be counted. An hour finder lights the number the hour hand has passed and outlines the one it is moving towards. A words card reads the time as minutes past the hour or minutes to the next hour. To draw a time, the hands are dragged: the minute hand snaps to a mark, and a ghost shows where the hour hand belongs for those minutes.
source_tool.art_direction: One exact clock face and its fives / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a clock face with sixty marks, a strip of the day from one midnight to the next, a ladder of units with tiles, the page's own timeline, a column frame, a time track with flags and a hopper, and a wall of month cards.

Every clock is drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees a minute and points exactly at a minute mark, and the hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree a minute, so it sits exactly where the time puts it and never on a number except at the hour.

The minute hand is always the longer hand and the hour hand the shorter, and a second hand, where there is one, is the thinnest. A clock face always shows all twelve numbers and all sixty marks, with a longer mark at each number.
A time in figures is written with a colon and a.m. or p.m., as 4:40 p.m., and a 24-hour time as four digits and the word hours, as 1615 hours. Twelve o'clock is written 12 noon or 12 midnight.
Noon and midnight are drawn as posts wherever a strip, a timeline or a track crosses them, and a.m. changes to p.m., or back, only at a post.
A column of time carries at sixty. A carried or broken hour or minute is drawn as sixty cells in six rows of ten, never as ten or as a hundred.
A month card is the real month of the year shown, with its first day under the right weekday and the right number of days, as the calendar in use today lays out that year.
Every day count shows which of its ends it counts. A day that is counted is filled, and a day that is left out is outlined only, at full strength and never hidden.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A hand, a column, a flag or a day is told apart by its shape, its label and its place first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a tile, a cell or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The hour hand, an hour tile, an hours column and the hours of a time split into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand and every minute are deep blue, and the second hand and every second are reddish purple, following the page, whose hour hand is red and whose second hand is a thin pink. The a.m. half of the day, midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on the duration track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile on the ladder are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Every clock rim, minute mark, number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket and guide line is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the fives again, up to the last number the minute hand has passed.
voice.onNext: A new clock. Find the minute hand before you read anything.
voice.opening: A clock with two hands, and a clock with figures. Where is each hand pointing?
voice.onFinish: Minutes counted in fives and then marks, and the hour read from the number the hand has passed.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any time on the clock, with the ring, the arc, the magnifier and the hour finder open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Each small mark is a minute
Counting on from the last number
The hour the hand has passed

placement.where: After each child has made a paper plate clock with sixty marks and two card hands, and set a few times on it by hand. The tool lights the fives and then the marks as a minute hand is read. It also shows exactly where the hour hand belongs for any minute, which a paper plate cannot check.

answer_key.rule: A digital clock shows the time in figures, and an analog clock shows it with hands. On an analog clock the space between two numbers is split into five equal parts by four small lines. The minute hand takes one minute to move from one mark to the next, so the sixty marks round the face make one hour. To read the minutes, count in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, then count the marks after it. The hour is the number the hour hand has passed, not the one it is moving towards; exactly on the hour, the hour hand is on the number. As the minutes pass, the hour hand moves from one number towards the next. It is a little way past the number early in the hour, and nearly at the next number late in the hour. A quarter past is fifteen minutes past the hour and half past is thirty. A quarter to is fifteen minutes before the next hour, which is forty-five minutes past the hour before it.
answer_key.wrong: The counting arc runs again from the twelve, lighting the fives and then the marks while they are counted aloud, and the hour finder lights the number the hour hand has passed. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A clock that shows the time in figures, with no hands, is a digital clock.
9:05 is five minutes past nine. Five minutes is one number round from the twelve, so the minute hand points at the one.
Nine o'clock has only just passed, so the hour hand has moved a little way past the nine.
items.answer: It is a digital clock. On an analog clock the minute hand points at the one, and the hour hand is just past the nine
items.question: A clock with no hands shows 9:05 in figures. What kind of clock is it, and where do the hands of an analog clock point at the same time?
items.checkpoint: A digital clock shows the time in figures and an analog clock shows it with hands, and both can show the same time to the minute.
items.misconception: Pointing the minute hand at the five for five minutes, or drawing the hour hand just before the nine, as if nine o'clock had not come.

steps: Between two numbers there are five small spaces, and the minute hand takes one minute to cross each one.
From the four to the seven the hand crosses three stretches: four to five, five to six and six to seven.
Three stretches of five spaces are fifteen spaces, so the hand takes fifteen minutes.
items.question: How many minutes does the minute hand take to move from the four to the seven?
items.checkpoint: Each small mark is one minute, and there are five of them from one number to the next.
items.misconception: Counting the four small lines between two numbers as four minutes, or saying three minutes because three numbers were passed.

steps: The six is the last number the minute hand has passed.
Count in fives to the six: five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty.
Then count the four marks after it: thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four.
items.question: The minute hand points at the fourth small mark after the six. How many minutes past the hour is it?
items.checkpoint: Count in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, then count the marks after it.
items.misconception: Reading the six as six minutes and answering ten, instead of counting the six as thirty minutes.

steps: Count in fives to the eleven, fifty-five, and three marks more make fifty-eight minutes.
The hour hand is very close to the four, but it has not reached it. The last number it has passed is the three.
So the time is 3:58. Two more minutes bring the clock to four o'clock.
items.answer: 3:58, which is two minutes to four
items.question: The minute hand points at the third small mark after the eleven, and the hour hand is just before the four. What time is it?
items.checkpoint: The hour is the number the hour hand has passed, not the one it is nearly at.
items.misconception: Reading the hour as four because the hour hand is almost on the four, and writing 4:58.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: An analog clock and a digital clock both show twenty past eleven. What does the digital clock show?
How many small marks does the minute hand pass in going once round the face, and how long does that take?
items.final_answer: Sixty marks, which take sixty minutes, or one hour

items.question: The minute hand moves from the two to the nine. How many minutes pass?
items.final_answer: Thirty-five minutes, because seven stretches of five marks are thirty-five marks

items.question: The minute hand is two marks past the ten. How many minutes past the hour is it?
items.final_answer: Fifty-two minutes: the ten stands for fifty, and two marks more make fifty-two

items.question: Where does the minute hand point at 6:18?
items.final_answer: At the third small mark after the three, because the three stands for fifteen minutes and three marks more make eighteen

items.question: The hour hand is between the ten and the eleven, and the minute hand shows forty-one minutes. What time is it?
items.final_answer: 10:41, because the hour hand has passed the ten and not yet reached the eleven

items.question: Set a clock to 12:56. Where do the two hands point?
items.final_answer: The minute hand points at the first small mark after the eleven. The hour hand is between the twelve and the one, almost at the one, because one o'clock has not yet come

items.question: A clock shows a quarter to six. A child writes the time as 6:45. What should it be, and why?
items.final_answer: 5:45. A quarter to six is fifteen minutes before six o'clock, so the hour hand has passed the five and not yet reached the six

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drags round the face and snaps to a minute mark
drags between the numbers, with a ghost showing where it belongs for the minutes set
shows the same time in figures, and can be covered
numbers the long marks five, ten, fifteen and on to sixty, shown or hidden
lights the fives to the last number passed, then each mark after it
spreads the space between two numbers apart so its five spaces can be counted
lights the number the hour hand has passed and outlines the one it is moving towards
reads the time as minutes past the hour or minutes to the next hour

teaching_notes: Make paper plate clocks before the tool is opened, with sixty marks and two card hands of different lengths, and set times on them in pairs. The section is called time to the exact minute, but its clocks are not drawn to the exact minute. Its worked clock says forty-eight minutes with the hand drawn nearer the forty-seventh mark, and each exercise face sits up to a mark from the minute the key gives it. The book's key reads the first exercise face as 5:08, where the drawn hand is nearer 5:09. It also draws the hour hand of 9:06 just before the nine instead of just past it. So accept any reading of the printed faces within one minute, and use this tool's clocks, which are drawn exactly, to settle where a hand belongs. Two moves need saying aloud every time. Count the minutes in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, and never read that number as that many minutes. And read the hour the hour hand has passed: late in an hour it is almost on the next number, and the hour is still the one before. The recap's words name the next hour only when they say to, as in a quarter to four, which is 3:45.
generation_prompt: Build an analog clock tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A large clock face fills the left of the working area with twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and a longer mark at every number. A digital readout sits beside it with a cover that slides over it. The minute hand is long and the hour hand short. Both are drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees for each minute and always points exactly at a mark. The hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree for each minute, so at any minute it sits exactly where the time puts it. The minute hand drags round and snaps to the nearest mark. The hour hand drags freely, and a faint ghost shows where it belongs for the minutes set. A fives ring outside the face numbers the long marks five to sixty and can be hidden. A counting arc follows the minute hand, lighting the fives from the twelve to the last number passed and then each mark after it. A magnifier spreads the space between two numbers apart so its four lines and five spaces can be counted. An hour finder lights the number the hour hand has passed and outlines the one it is moving towards. A words card reads the time as minutes past or minutes to. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Count in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed. Then count the marks after it. Read the hour the hour hand has passed. Drag the hands to show a time.
